lede: Joins put tables side by side. Set operations stack them: everything from both, only what both have, or what one has that the other doesn't. They're the quickest way to compare two lists.
objectives: Stack DataFrames with `union`, and match columns by name with `unionByName`
Remove repeats with `distinct` when you want each value once
Find what two DataFrames share with `intersect` and what one lacks with `subtract`
Explain whole-row comparison, NULL matching and the `All` variants that keep duplicates

blocks.md:
`accounts` is a CRM snapshot taken on 1 January. `customer_cdc` is every change since then: updates, deletes and new accounts, one row per change. Both have an `account_id`.

`a.union(b)` returns the rows of `a` followed by the rows of `b`. The two must have the same number of columns. It keeps every row, repeats included; add `distinct()` when you want each row once.

blocks.title: Every account id, once
blocks.code:
snapshot_ids = accounts.select("account_id")
feed_ids = customer_cdc.select("account_id")

both = snapshot_ids.union(feed_ids)
print(snapshot_ids.count(), "+", feed_ids.count(), "=", both.count())

both.distinct().orderBy("account_id").show()
blocks.note: 15 rows stacked, 7 distinct accounts: the snapshot's five plus two added by the feed.

blocks.md: `union` matches columns **by position**, not by name. If the second DataFrame has its columns in another order, values land in the wrong column and Spark doesn't complain as long as the types fit. `unionByName` matches by name instead.

blocks.title: By position or by name
blocks.note: In the first result the feed's names sit under `account_id`. `unionByName` lines them up. With `allowMissingColumns=True` it also accepts columns that only one side has and fills the other side with NULL.

blocks.title: Different numbers of columns
blocks.note: Every set operation needs the same columns on both sides. Select them first so the two shapes match.

blocks.md: `a.intersect(b)` keeps the rows that appear in both. `a.subtract(b)` keeps the rows of `a` that don't appear in `b`; the order matters. Both return each row once.

blocks.title: In both, in one only
blocks.note: Four snapshot accounts changed, ACC-0005 didn't, and ACC-0006 and ACC-0007 are new. Three questions, three one-liners.

blocks.md:
Set operations compare **whole rows**: every column must be equal. One different value, like an updated credit limit, makes two rows different. Unlike a join, two NULLs count as equal here, so a missing value can match a missing value.

A delete in the feed carries the last row before the delete, so only that row still equals its snapshot row.

blocks.title: Whole rows, and repeats
blocks.note: Only ACC-0003 is unchanged in the feed. ACC-0001 has two invoices: `subtract` removes it entirely, while `exceptAll` takes away one copy per matching row and leaves one. `intersectAll` keeps repeats the same way.

concept.prompt: `a` has columns `(id, name)` and `b` has `(name, id)`, both strings. What does `a.union(b)` do?
choices: Stacks them by position, so b's names end up in the id column
Keeps only rows that appear in both
concept.why: `union` matches by position. Use `unionByName` to match by column name.

concept.prompt: `x` has the ids `A` and NULL; `y` has NULL and `B`. What does `x.intersect(y)` return?
choices: No rows: NULL never equals NULL
concept.why: Set operations treat two NULLs as equal, so the NULL row is in both. An inner join on the same column would match nothing.

concept.prompt: `a` has the id ACC-0001 twice and `b` has it once. What does `a.exceptAll(b)` return?
concept.why: `exceptAll` removes one copy per matching row in `b`, leaving one. `subtract` would remove it completely.

review: `union` stacks rows by position and keeps repeats; add `distinct()` to keep each row once.
`unionByName` matches columns by name; `allowMissingColumns=True` fills missing ones with NULL.
`intersect` keeps rows in both; `subtract` keeps rows of the first that aren't in the second. Both remove repeats.
Set operations compare whole rows and treat two NULLs as equal.
Both sides need the same number of columns, with compatible types: select the columns first.
